brief.head: The whipped creme
brief.text: Ajay Shah ques­tioned the nar­row­ness of the so-called creme of the coun­try. “When I was in IIT,” he re­called, “we used to be called the whipped creme.” {070-J04}

brief.head: Fastest gun
brief.text: Coaching classes re­duce the exam to 1,700 ques­tion types, Ajay Shah said. A drilled top­per is quick “not be­cause you’re so smart, but be­cause you’ve seen them be­fore”. {070-J05}

brief.head: Mind the bureaucrats
brief.text: Amit Varma: “Never trust a joint sec­re­tary.” Ajay Shah: “Education is too im­por­tant to be left to ed­u­ca­tion bu­reau­crats.” Both were ob­ject­ing to one na­tional pol­icy for every col­lege. {070-J08}

brief.head: The English advantage
brief.text: Interviews beat marks alone, Amit Varma agreed, but they mas­sively favour the priv­i­leged who grew up speak­ing English at home. He would weigh sev­eral fac­tors in­stead. {#english}

brief.head: Robots, not marks
brief.text: Kavi Arya’s E-Yantra chal­lenges stu­dents to build a robot that does X. With no cer­tifi­cate, exam or marks, Ajay Shah said, the only re­ward is the plea­sure of doing it. {070-R14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s entrance exams
lead.head: Many are coached, few are chosen

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 70

play.label: Hear the case step by step

body: Amit Varma says he chose his co-host by en­trance exam. It had one mul­ti­ple-choice ques­tion, and Ajay Shah, of­fered all the money and fame in the world, a pri­vate jet or Instagram star­dom, picked “free­dom for ev­ery­one”. {070-J01}
India’s real en­trance exams, the hosts agreed, are no joke. “In India, this is a bloody mess,” Shah said. “Everything about it is bro­ken.”
There are very few seats and in­sane lev­els of com­pe­ti­tion, he said. A whole in­dus­try teaches to the test, the stress is high, and stu­dents try the exams for years.

Varma lo­cated the heart of it in a mis­match of sup­ply and de­mand: very few seats, and many, many stu­dents who want them. Coaching in­sti­tutes are ev­ery­where. “Every year you hear about sui­cides in Kota,” he said. “It has be­come an in­dus­try.”
## The myth of merit
Shah went after the claim that gives the sys­tem its moral le­git­i­macy: that more marks in the JEE mean more in­tel­li­gence and more knowl­edge. “I no longer be­lieve that,” he said.

A high-stakes exam has only so many ques­tion types, he ar­gued, so coach­ing turns it into pat­tern recog­ni­tion. “It is un­in­tel­li­gent in ex­actly the way that com­puter sys­tems are un­in­tel­li­gent,” he said. {070-C02}

The one trait it re­wards is con­sci­en­tious­ness: chil­dren who obey, drill from morn­ing to night and shut out every other kind of knowl­edge. India, Shah said, is mis­al­lo­cat­ing its scarce seats.
## Within the sys­tem

Varma posed what he calls Varma’s Question: where is the co­er­cion? {070-C01} There is none in chil­dren going to coach­ing classes, he said. They are the market’s an­swer to a bro­ken sys­tem, and ban­ning them would be ab­surd.

Shah of­fered three fixes that work within the par­a­digm. Run com­put­erised tests, drawn at ran­dom from a ques­tion bank, about 250 days a year, and count each candidate’s best of two or three at­tempts. Make the tests adapt to the can­di­date. Hand the work to pri­vate firms.
Going deeper, Shah ar­gued that col­leges should be free to choose their own stu­dents and to look at the whole per­son, as the IIMs do with group dis­cus­sions and in­ter­views.
## A friendly fight

Then came what Varma billed as the masala. Shah and Nitin Pai pro­pose an exam at about 17 to find the top one lakh stu­dents, then a lot­tery among them for the 20,000 IIT seats. Parents, Shah said, need not bother with Kota. {070-C07}
Varma was not hav­ing it. “I have great fond­ness for both you and Nitin and great re­spect,” he said. “But in this mat­ter, you are both wrong.”
The plan, he said, was “an ex­cel­lent tech­no­cratic de­sign of a bad so­lu­tion”. It missed the point: there are not enough seats.

“Today ev­ery­one in India who wants to get a sham­poo can buy a sham­poo,” Varma said. Good ed­u­ca­tion, by con­trast, is kept scarce by the state, through li­cences, a ban on profit, land rules and PhD re­quire­ments for fac­ulty. Shah agreed, adding that only politi­cians start uni­ver­si­ties in India.

For par­ents and stu­dents, Shah’s ad­vice was to look past the brand names of IIT and MIT, and at the per­son in the mir­ror. Checking out of the rat race, he said, “should be per­fectly okay”. {070-C12}
His ideal is a child who grows up ex­cited and happy, per­haps tak­ing an in­ter­est in or­ganic chem­istry or the elec­tric gui­tar, and who knows about the world.

second.label: Testing, statistically
second.head: Not an objective truth
second.deck: Ajay Shah wants India’s exams built by statisticians, one question at a time

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the exam as a statistical estimator

body: “An exam is not an ob­jec­tive truth,” Ajay Shah said. “An exam is a sta­tis­ti­cal es­ti­ma­tor of the knowl­edge of the test taker.” So look for its bias and its error vari­ance, he ar­gued, and work to re­duce both. {070-C04}

His tool is item re­sponse the­ory, used in the GRE and the SAT: easy ques­tions first, harder ones once you ace them. In India, Shah said, where some 1 per cent get through, it is the top tail that must be told apart. {#onepercent}

Each reused ques­tion goes under the mi­cro­scope: if strong can­di­dates do not get it right more often than weak ones, the ques­tion is faulty. As for UPSC pa­pers, Shah said, “they are non­sense”. {#upsc}

quote.text: We should not be so rev­er­en­tial about these exams.

third.head: Lights, camera, lecture

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on knowledge without the credential

body: Amit Varma will not call it a so­lu­tion, be­cause so­lu­tions go to root causes. It is a ju­gaadu hack. “Put one frickin’ video cam­era, record it, put it on­line,” he urged every col­lege. {#camera}
Teachers would feel more ac­count­able, he said. Those who did not make it through would still get the knowl­edge, if not the net­work or the cre­den­tials.
His ex­am­ple is Robert Sapolsky’s bi­ol­ogy lec­tures, free on YouTube. Varma had never been in­ter­ested in bi­ol­ogy, he said, but Sapolsky “just opens your mind up in dif­fer­ent ways”. {070-R10}

Ajay Shah said IIT Bombay al­ready does this, tak­ing its en­gi­neer­ing teach­ing on video to hun­dreds of thou­sands of stu­dents. “If there is knowl­edge in­side IIT Bombay, it is avail­able,” he said. “The rest is just cre­den­tial­ism and is less im­por­tant.” {070-C11}

p2.title: The fix is in
p2.deck: From the myth of merit to the root cause, Ajay Shah’s reforms and Amit Varma’s objections, chapter by chapter

from1.head: Many are coached, few are chosen

quote.text: We are not get­ting the best kids into the IITs. We are get­ting the kids who have the abil­ity to be reg­i­mented.

box.title: The paper behind the fight
box.text: Ajay Shah’s lot­tery plan is set out in *Doing better than a competitive exam*, writ­ten with Nitin Pai. The two drew on ideas from all over the world, Shah said, and adapted them to Indian con­di­tions. {#pai}

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Merit by rote
sections.caption: the meritocracy myth
body: The system’s moral le­git­i­macy, Ajay Shah said, rests on one claim: that the stu­dent with more marks in the IIT JEE is more in­tel­li­gent, more knowl­edge­able and bet­ter suited to an en­gi­neer­ing ed­u­ca­tion. “I no longer be­lieve all these things,” he said.

His rea­son is the high-stakes exam it­self. A school-leaving test can ask only so much of a twelfth-standard child, so coach­ing classes an­a­lyse past pa­pers and boil it down to 1,700 ques­tion types. Work two days on each, and in 3,400 days you are ready. {#types}
What re­sults is table lookup: see this type of ques­tion, jump to that so­lu­tion. It is un­in­tel­li­gent, Shah said, in ex­actly the way that com­put­ers are. {070-C02}
## One trait among many

Human ca­pa­bil­ity, he ar­gued, is cu­rios­ity, tenac­ity, in­no­va­tion, cre­ativ­ity and flex­i­ble gen­eral in­tel­li­gence. The exam re­wards only con­sci­en­tious­ness: chil­dren who obey, work from morn­ing to night and “just mem­o­rise the re­ac­tions of ben­zene”. {#benzene}

Each fam­ily is be­hav­ing sen­si­bly, Shah granted: in a so­ci­ety of cre­den­tial­ism, chas­ing an IIT de­gree is in­cen­tive com­pat­i­ble. But the coun­try mis­al­lo­cates its seats, and its children’s hours.

~ Amit Varma agreed. The exam, he said, has be­come a game within a game, about ad­mis­sions rather than knowl­edge: “We have two seats and eighty-five peo­ple who want to be in those two seats.” {#twoseats}

quote.text: We are not get­ting the best kids into the IITs. We are get­ting the kids who have the abil­ity to be reg­i­mented.

sections.label: Varma’s question
sections.head: Don’t ban the paracetamol
sections.caption: banning the coaching classes
body: Ajay Shah, needling, of­fered an easy way out. “Our dear friend Xi Jinping” had shut down China’s en­tire test-prep in­dus­try in one fell swoop. Free mar­kets are all very well, he teased, “but in this one case, you’ve re­ally got to give it be­cause of the plight of the chil­dren.” {070-J02}

Amit Varma called it an ab­surd so­lu­tion, and an­swered with Varma’s Question: where is the co­er­cion? Not in the coach­ing classes, he said. Children go be­cause the sys­tem de­mands it of them, and the mar­ket serves them. {070-C01}
## Fever and pills

Suppose you run a fever of 103 every day and end up tak­ing three parac­eta­mols a day. “Is the so­lu­tion to this ban­ning parac­eta­mols? Of course not,” Varma said. You find what is caus­ing the fever. {070-C03}

Banning a vic­tim­less ac­tiv­ity, he ar­gued, merely drives it un­der­ground. Prohibit liquor and it comes from the black mar­ket, dearer and worse, and peo­ple die of hooch poi­son­ing. A ban on pros­ti­tu­tion brings traf­fick­ing and co­er­cion.
~ The real co­er­cion, Varma promised, lay some­where else, and he would get to it by the end of the episode.

quote.text: Whenever there is a prob­lem in so­ci­ety or pub­lic pol­icy, the first ques­tion I want to ask is where is the co­er­cion?

sections.label: Three quick fixes
sections.head: Every day is exam day
sections.caption: the three-part solution
body: Staying in­side the par­a­digm, Ajay Shah of­fered three fixes. The first ends the sin­gle exam on a sin­gle day, which today sends two and a half mil­lion chil­dren to test cen­tres across the coun­try. {#onesingle}

States learn only by doing things re­peat­edly, he said. So run a com­put­erised test, gen­er­ated at run­time from a large ques­tion bank, for 250 days a year: 10,000 can­di­dates a day. Let each take it two or three times and keep the best score, in case of a heat wave, bad air or a bad day. {070-C05}
None of it is new. Shah had helped NSE build just such an exam for de­riv­a­tives traders, and ETS runs the SAT and GRE this way.
## Better maths, pri­vate hands

The sec­ond fix is item re­sponse the­ory, which ad­justs the ques­tions to the can­di­date. The third is to let pri­vate firms run the tests, since gov­ern­ments, Shah said, are not good at run­ning air­lines, pay­ment sys­tems or banks. {#private}
~ Amit Varma loved all of it, and was re­minded of his chess puz­zles. His one caveat: these were “fan­tas­tic tech­no­cratic so­lu­tions” that did not reach the root cause.

quote.text: It’s much bet­ter to do things re­peat­edly and mis­takes will hap­pen and there will be feed­back loops and you’ll get things bet­ter.

sections.label: Free the colleges
sections.head: Berkeley is not Los Angeles
sections.caption: letting colleges pick their students
body: The most im­por­tant piece, Ajay Shah said, is to end cen­tral­i­sa­tion. A uni­ver­sity gets bet­ter only when it has au­ton­omy, a sense of mis­sion and the power to make its own de­ci­sions, year after year.
It is as wrong to force all the IITs to be alike, he ar­gued, as to run every pub­lic sec­tor bank as one. {070-C06}
Admission to the University of California, Berkeley is fully dis­tinct from ad­mis­sion to its Los Angeles sib­ling, Shah pointed out, though both sit in the state’s UC sys­tem. {#berkeley}

A mo­ti­vated uni­ver­sity can cal­i­brate CBSE marks against ICSE ones, he said, and the Los Angeles cam­pus com­pares ap­pli­cants from every school sys­tem in the world. “It’s not that hard to fig­ure out who is a good can­di­date.”
## See the whole per­son
Shah wants India out of the test men­tal­ity. The IIMs use a group dis­cus­sion and an in­ter­view, and eco­nom­ics PhD ad­mis­sions now in­clude a video in­ter­view. {#iims}
Amit Varma agreed, with a caveat: in­ter­views favour the priv­i­leged who grew up speak­ing English at home, so they work best as one fac­tor among sev­eral.
~ Colleges, Varma said, should be able to com­pete on how well they se­lect bright peo­ple. One might want a lib­eral-arts bent, Shah added, an­other a busi­ness-school one.

quote.text: It is ex­actly as wrong to try to force all the IITs to be alike or all uni­ver­si­ties in India to be alike.

sections.label: The lottery
sections.head: Luck of the draw
sections.caption: the Pai-Shah lottery
body: Ajay Shah and Nitin Pai pro­pose two stages. First, an all-India con­cep­tual exam at about 17, hard to game with test prep, in which the goal is the top one lakh rather than the top thou­sand. {#toplakh}

Shah pegged the bar at roughly 650 on the OECD’s PISA test, which he called more con­cep­tual and not some­thing you can train for. Then the 20,000 IIT seats are drawn by lot­tery from the one lakh. {#stage2}

He saw three gains: more var­ied IIT batches, pro­fes­sors forced to raise their teach­ing, and 80,000 strong stu­dents lift­ing class­rooms across India. A nor­mal school ed­u­ca­tion, plus foot­ball and cu­rios­ity, would be enough. {070-C07}
## You are both wrong

Amit Varma, who had promised a fight, said the plan was being com­pared in an ide­alised form with the real sys­tem. It does not re­ward de­sire or hard work, he said: for some, the top one lakh “would just be a breeze”.

Then there is al­lo­ca­tion. A child des­per­ate to study me­chan­i­cal en­gi­neer­ing could lose out to one who wants to write poems, “and both of us will be mis­er­able for the rest of our lives”. {#poems}
~ Similar lot­ter­ies for medicine in the Netherlands and New Zealand, Varma said, have drawn crit­i­cism.

quote.text: The scheme that you laid out with the num­bers that you laid out are an ex­cel­lent tech­no­cratic de­sign of a bad so­lu­tion

sections.label: The root cause
sections.head: Shampoo galore, seats rationed
sections.caption: where the coercion lies
body: “Today ev­ery­one in India who wants to get a sham­poo can buy a sham­poo,” Amit Varma said. Education, by con­trast, is kept scarce, and India has nor­malised it. {070-C09}

Offered the post of dic­ta­tor by Ajay Shah, Varma balked: a dic­ta­tor, he said, makes a good so­lu­tion im­pos­si­ble. {070-J07} Then he an­swered his own ques­tion: the co­er­cion comes from the state, stand­ing in the way of pri­vate en­trepreneurs who would set up col­leges.

To start one, you need li­cences and per­mis­sions that can take years. Land and in­fra­struc­ture man­dates fol­low, and rules that fac­ulty must hold PhDs. Hiring Varma, who has none, to teach pod­cast­ing or writ­ing should be a “no-brainer”, he said. {#podcasting}
## A dirty word

Then there is the man­date that higher ed­u­ca­tion can­not be run for profit. Founders re­sort to ju­gaad with trusts, at great fric­tion and cost. “To me, profit is the best kind of phi­lan­thropy,” Varma said, be­cause in a free mar­ket you profit only by mak­ing some­one bet­ter off. {070-C10}

Shah agreed. Because start­ing a uni­ver­sity is so hard, only politi­cians do it, and they are not the peo­ple best equipped to. {#politicians} He is op­ti­mistic about Ashoka, FLAME and Nayanta, but asked why so few are al­lowed.
~ The same holds for medicine, Shah said: India sim­ply does not have enough med­i­cal col­leges.

quote.text: We have nor­malised the fact that good qual­ity ed­u­ca­tion is a scarce re­source.
These are human be­ings and we need to nur­ture and grow their in­tel­lec­tual and emo­tional ca­pac­ity. That’s what grow­ing up is about. That’s what ed­u­ca­tion is about.

p3.title: Tales from the exam hall
p3.deck: A swimming test, a chess rating, a teenage hacker and a traders’ exam

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a thought experiment from Deepak VS
stories.head: Sink or swim into the IITs
body: Deepak VS, a friend of both hosts and a guest on Amit Varma’s pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen*, is al­ways throw­ing out thought ex­per­i­ments. On that show he once threw a hy­po­thet­i­cal at Varma: scrap the IIT en­trance exam, and re­place it with a swim­ming test. {070-S04}
Varma brought it up in the mid­dle of his fight with Ajay Shah over Shah’s lot­tery for IIT seats. It was re­lated, he said, though not one of his crit­i­cisms.
There was a logic to the swim­ming test. In Varma’s words, you would at least be se­lect­ing for de­sire. India has coast­line across the coun­try, and could set up swim­ming pools.
Such thought ex­per­i­ments, he said, are a great way to de­nor­malise things and think about them.

Then came the twist. “Now ob­vi­ously year two, year three, ev­ery­thing goes to hell,” Varma said. Coaching classes start, and the whole busi­ness gets in­sti­tu­tion­alised, with “IIT coaches and Speedos on bill­boards”.
Before long, he said, “you have the same prob­lems that we have with the cur­rent sys­tem”. The dis­ease, as he would argue later in the episode, is the scarcity of seats, not the par­tic­u­lar test.

~ Varma had made a sim­i­lar joke at the very start. If Shah said any­thing against free­dom, he warned, he might have to fire him and hold an­other en­trance exam for a co-host, “and now ev­ery­body will game it be­cause they know the an­swer”. {#game}
stories.why: Any sin­gle high-stakes fil­ter guard­ing a scarce prize gets gamed by an in­dus­try built around it. Swap the exam for a swim and the coach­ing fol­lows, Speedos and all. Varma’s an­swer is more seats. {070-C09}
stories.postscript: Varma rec­om­mended his con­ver­sa­tion with Deepak VS, *Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face*, for more such thought ex­per­i­ments.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the swimming test

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on chess puzzles and adaptive testing
stories.head: Grandmaster, on paper
body: Ajay Shah’s idea of a test that adapts to the can­di­date re­minded Amit Varma of a de­light­ful ses­sion at his lap­top, solv­ing chess puz­zles on chess.com while Shah sat be­side him.
The site works the way Shah wants exams to work. As your rat­ing rises, the puz­zles get tougher; slip, and they get eas­ier. That day, Varma reached 2900. {070-S01}

“With great awe in your eyes,” Varma re­minded Shah, “you asked that, I mean, does this mean that you’re equal to a 2900 in the real world.” It did not. His ac­tual rat­ing, he said, is around 1900 to 2000. {#elo}
~ Shah held that 2900 was still super cool. Varma was un­moved: there is mas­sive in­fla­tion in puz­zle rat­ings, “so it’s not that cool”.
stories.why: A score means some­thing only rel­a­tive to what it mea­sures. A puz­zle rat­ing that rises and falls with each an­swer is a fa­mil­iar ver­sion of the adap­tive test­ing Shah wants for India’s en­trance exams. {070-C04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the chess.com puzzle rating

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an exam that asked about his hobbies
stories.head: The boy who hacked circuits
body: Long ago, Ajay Shah re­called, India had an exam called the NTS, the National Talent Search. As he re­mem­bered it, a third of the weight went to an IQ test, a third to a bunch of sub­jects and a third to an in­ter­view.
So a panel sat Shah down, a tenth-standard child, and asked what he did in his spare time. “I hack elec­tronic cir­cuitry,” he said. {070-S02}
“So they said, Tell us about your elec­tronic cir­cuitry.” That, Shah said, is the right way to talk to a child of that age, “not just like grind them into an exam”.
~ If the IIMs can weigh in­ter­views and group dis­cus­sions, he asked, why can’t the IIT en­trance? {#iims}
stories.why: India once ran a high-stakes se­lec­tion that treated a teenager as a whole per­son, not a ma­chine for pro­duc­ing marks. Shah’s point is that ad­mis­sion to the IITs could also look be­yond a sin­gle test.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the National Talent Search interview

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a reform India has already tried
stories.head: Book a slot, sit the test
body: Many years ago, Ajay Shah helped NSE build a cer­ti­fi­ca­tion exam for traders who wanted to do de­riv­a­tive trad­ing.

Test-taking cen­tres were set up all over the coun­try. “We de­vel­oped a ques­tion bank once,” he said, “and then a ran­dom sub­set of those ques­tions is shown to each per­son.” Candidates booked an ap­point­ment and took the test when­ever they pleased. {070-S03}
Shah told the story to show that his first re­form for India’s en­trance exams, a com­put­erised test that runs all year, is noth­ing new, and has been run in India be­fore.
~ The SAT and the GRE, he noted, al­ready run this way, through a pri­vate firm called ETS. “I’m not say­ing any­thing novel,” he said. {#ets}
stories.why: The ob­sta­cle to bet­ter exams, the story sug­gests, is not tech­ni­cal know-how. It is the habit of hold­ing one giant state-run exam on one sin­gle day, for two and a half mil­lion chil­dren. {#onesingle}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the NSE certification exam

quiz.a: None of these, but free­dom for ev­ery­one, over money, fame, a jet or Instagram.

quiz.q: What is Varma’s Question, which Amit Varma asks first of any problem in society or policy?
quiz.a: Where is the co­er­cion? The an­swer usu­ally points to the problem’s root cause.

quiz.q: Why would Varma not ban coaching classes, judging by his analogy of a daily fever of 103?
quiz.a: You don’t ban parac­eta­mol for a fever; you find what is caus­ing it.

quiz.q: In the Pai-Shah plan, how many qualify in stage one, and how are IIT seats allotted?
quiz.a: The top one lakh qual­ify, then the 20,000 IIT seats are drawn by lot­tery.

quiz.q: Which old exam gave a third of its weight to an interview, as Ajay Shah remembers it?
quiz.a: The National Talent Search, whose panel asked him what he did in his spare time.

quiz.q: What has India normalised, according to Varma, even as everyone can buy a shampoo?
quiz.a: That good qual­ity ed­u­ca­tion is a scarce re­source, ra­tioned through en­trance exams.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 70. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Xi Jinping (Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain); Robert Sapolsky (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Doing better than a competitive exam
shelf.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Nitin Pai and Ajay’s case against or­gan­is­ing Indian ed­u­ca­tion around sin­gle exams like UPSC, IIT-JEE and the boards, with a pro­posal: a con­cep­tual exam to qual­ify the top one lakh stu­dents, then a lot­tery for IIT seats.

shelf.title: Rethinking NEET, and medical education
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ap­plies the episode’s ar­gu­ment to med­i­cal ad­mis­sions, where Ajay says the root cause is the lack of med­i­cal col­leges.

shelf.title: Diluting the role of the IIT JEE
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It shows Ajay has been ar­gu­ing for years against the JEE as the be-all and end-all.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face (Episode 373 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Deepak VS
shelf.why: Deepak VS, an en­tre­pre­neur in his mid-twenties whom Amit calls an in­cred­i­bly fine thinker, is al­ways throw­ing out thought ex­per­i­ments that de­nor­malise things; he pointed out that any new en­trance test would be gamed within a year.

shelf.title: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what’s bro­ken in Indian ed­u­ca­tion and how to fix it, in­clud­ing his point that the sys­tem is op­ti­mised for sort­ing, not teach­ing.

shelf.title: Education in India (Episode 77 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Amit Chandra
shelf.why: An ear­lier long-form con­ver­sa­tion with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian ed­u­ca­tion, an­other field the hosts say suf­fers from keep­ing prices out.

shelf.title: The Medical Council of India (Episode 8 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath
shelf.why: It looks at the reg­u­la­tor side of the sup­ply short­age that drives the crazi­ness of med­i­cal en­trance exams.

shelf.title: Robert Sapolsky’s biology lectures on YouTube
shelf.creator: Robert Sapolsky
shelf.why: Sapolsky’s class­room lec­tures are free on­line and, in Amit’s words, ab­so­lutely mas­ter­ful.

shelf.title: Behave
shelf.creator: Robert Sapolsky
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky’s mas­ter­pieces and a bril­liant book.

shelf.title: Determined
shelf.creator: Robert Sapolsky
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky’s mas­ter­pieces and a bril­liant book.

shelf.title: Educational Outreach, IIT Bombay (CDEEP)
shelf.creator: D. B. Phatak and others at IIT Bombay
shelf.why: It records IIT Bombay’s en­gi­neer­ing teach­ing on video and takes it to hun­dreds of thou­sands of stu­dents across India.

shelf.title: E-Yantra
shelf.creator: Kavi Arya
shelf.why: It re­places exam ques­tions with cre­ative chal­lenges like ‘build me a robot that does X’.

laughs.text: The cold open: Amit says he picked his co-host through an en­trance exam with one mul­ti­ple-choice ques­tion. The op­tions were all the money in the world; all the fame with groupies (‘Even the thought could get you canceled’); a pri­vate jet and a house in the Bahamas; be­com­ing the world’s big­gest Instagram in­flu­encer; or ‘none of these, but free­dom for ev­ery­one.’ ‘And Ajay Shah chose free­dom for ev­ery­one, and that’s why we’re here today. Well done, you aced the en­trance test.’ Later Amit warns Ajay not to say any­thing against free­dom, or he’ll have to hold an­other en­trance exam, ‘and now ev­ery­body will game it be­cause they know the an­swer.’

Ajay baits Amit with a mock big-state pitch: ‘our dear friend Xi Jinping’ shut down China’s whole test-prep in­dus­try in one fell swoop, ‘like free mar­kets and all that is good. But in this one case, you’ve re­ally got to give it be­cause of the plight of the chil­dren. Like come on, where will the chil­dren go?’ Amit: ‘You’re try­ing to nee­dle nee­dle nee­dle me.’
Amit catches a slight smile on Ajay’s face as he says ‘IIT en­trance exams’, re­mem­ber­ing that he too cleared it, and asks ed­i­tor Nomsita MS Haritashya to re­play the clip: ‘I did not miss that.’
Ajay on the self-image of IITians as the ‘creme of the country’: ‘When I was in IIT we used to be called the whipped creme.’

Amit hypes the next seg­ment: ‘you want Masala, get your pop­corn, we are gonna fight here.’ He then de­liv­ers the ver­dict on the Pai-Shah lot­tery: ‘I have great fond­ness for both you and Nitin and great re­spect. But in this mat­ter, you are both wrong.’

Amit passes on a friend’s jibe about Ashoka University stu­dents and asks if it’s true. Ajay warns that many Ashoka stu­dents are the show’s au­di­ence, ‘so you bet­ter be nice to them,’ and Amit im­me­di­ately with­draws his state­ment.

Kota, the coach­ing-class hub where kids are sent from 8th stan­dard, ‘Every year you hear about sui­cides in Kota, it has be­come an in­dus­try.’ Also men­tioned: Irodov and Resnick and Halliday, the physics books every JEE as­pi­rant grinds through.

ETS, the pri­vate firm be­hind the SAT and GRE, which al­ready run con­tin­u­ous, adap­tive, ques­tion-bank-based tests. OECD PISA, a test for 15-year-olds that Ajay calls more con­cep­tual and not some­thing you can train for, is his bench­mark for the pro­posed el­i­gi­bil­ity exam.
‘You don’t throw the baby out with the bath­wa­ter, as it were, old German saying’ — Amit, ar­gu­ing against ban­ning coach­ing classes.
